input.command:
cd /Users/suhaan/devenv/p0p1/p1-new
gh pr comment 85 --repo entireio/entire-brain --body 'Pushed `c7ce1b19` + `f59c760d`. This closes the three review items that were left open by design, fixes a defect I introduced in the previous round, removes a per-sync network round-trip, and de-flakes two load-sensitive brief tests. Every fix has a test that fails when the fix is reverted.

## Review items 3, 4 and 5 — now closed

**4. `distill --force` silently deleted cross-member conflicts.** The final flush dropped the *whole* local review queue. Dropping distill'"'"'s own backlog is right — the rebuild regenerates it — but the queue is shared, and conflicts raised by `facts sync` are never regenerated, so they vanished with no trace and nobody could review them. Ownership is the `ProposedBy` attribution (the same rule the publish filter already uses): distill'"'"'s entries carry none, sync-raised ones do. A force rebuild now drops only what it owns.

**5. An orphaned proposal could not be removed.** One whose fact head is gone entirely cannot be accepted, and reject was blocked too: the empty-head guard returned before the reject path, and pushing an empty fact set is refused on purpose. Reject changes no facts, so the write it actually needs is the proposal set alone — expressed as `FactsUnchanged`, which CASes the set and leaves the head at `factsOldRef`. Pairing it with accept is refused outright, so it can never become a way to retire a proposal while dropping its merge result.

**3. Settled conflicts came back in a second clone.** Publication was suppressed only by the shared-proposal ledger, which lives in one checkout, so another clone of the same member started empty and republished conflicts the team had already resolved. This did not need the server-side tombstone the review suggested: the shared head is identical for every clone, and a settled conflict is no longer *applicable* to it, so applicability now gates publication regardless of ledger state.

## A defect I introduced in the previous round

Mirroring settlements created a way to lose them. With no readable shared head there is nothing to mirror *from*, yet the settled entry was still pruned — leaving the retired fact active locally with no record left to reconcile it against, reintroducing the exact defect the mirroring exists to close. Such entries now stay queued until they can actually be mirrored, and mirroring precedes the prune so a crash retries instead of losing it.

## Performance

`Sync` already computes the post-sync fact set, so it now returns it. Callers needing the head — to check which proposals are still live, or to mirror settlements — use that instead of a second `Current`, **removing a full network round-trip from every sync against a hosted backend**. A no-op reject also no longer rewrites the fact store or bumps the source manifest.

## Accuracy

After `facts proposals apply`, the member'"'"'s own local facts now reflect their decision immediately, in the same write lock that prunes the local copy. Previously the member who made the call kept seeing the pre-settlement state in their own recall until their next sync.

## Two load-sensitive brief tests

`TestBrainBriefGitIntentLiveShapedOperationalRecall` failed a full-suite run alongside a `-race` run **on correct code**. It drives real git through `ExecRunner`, and the overlay is bounded at 500 ms on purpose — it degrades to the baseline rather than letting a slow repo stall a brief. Under load the two git calls miss that window, the overlay correctly returns false, and the assertion that it *must* activate fails. Now retried a bounded five times; verified it still catches real breakage by stubbing the promoter to return false. The hard-timeout case budgeted `timeout + 500 ms` = 1 s total; since the runner blocks on `ctx.Done()` a broken bound never returns at all rather than returning late, so the slack only has to exclude that.

Worth stating plainly: that 500 ms bound means the git-intent overlay also stops contributing on a loaded machine **in production**, not only in tests. The code comment shows it is a deliberate trade, so I have left the product behavior alone rather than trading latency for it uninvited.

## Audited, no change needed

The privacy-purge and hosted-settle queue writers both drop only what they should — proposals whose facts were deleted, and exactly the settled id.

## Verification

`gofmt -s`, `go vet ./...`, `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...` clean; `go test ./...` green across all 9 packages; `-race` clean on `factsync`, `factmerge`, `brainwire`, `hostedbrain`, `factgitmeta`.

## Correction to this PR'"'"'s description

The body says shared publication is blocked on an entiredb reserved-ref unblock. **That is stale.** `refs/meta/entire/*` has a registered workload writer (`WorkloadEntireAPI`, ENT-1106) and `server/githttp/receive_pack.go` states other `refs/meta/*` paths were never reserved — "standard git-meta clients can push them directly". Nothing in entiredb blocks this any more.' 2>&1 | tail -2

Everything is on **#85** (`+7,065/−27`, 22 files). Waiting on CI to confirm green.

## What landed

**The three review items left open — closed:**
- **`distill --force` silently deleted cross-member conflicts.** It dropped the whole shared queue; distill may only drop what it *owns* (unattributed entries). Sync-raised ones it never regenerates, so they vanished unreviewed.
- **Orphaned proposals were unremovable.** Couldn't be accepted (no head) and couldn't be rejected either (the guard fired first). Reject changes no facts, so it now writes only the proposal set via `FactsUnchanged` — refused outright if paired with accept.
- **Settled conflicts resurrected in a second clone.** This *didn't* need the server-side tombstone the review proposed: the shared head is identical across clones and a settled conflict is no longer applicable to it, so applicability gates publication regardless of the per-checkout ledger.

**A defect I introduced last round:** mirroring created a way to *lose* settlements — with no readable head there's nothing to mirror from, yet the entry was still pruned. Entries now stay queued until they can actually be mirrored.

**Performance:** `Sync` already computes the post-sync head, so it returns it — **removing a full network round-trip from every hosted sync.** Plus no more pointless fact-store write on a no-op reject.

**Accuracy:** `facts proposals apply` now mirrors into the member's own facts immediately, instead of leaving their recall contradicting the decision they just made until the next sync.

**A test failed my verification on correct code, and the root cause is a real product characteristic.** The git-intent overlay is bounded at 500ms by design; under load real git misses that window, the overlay correctly degrades, and a test requiring activation fails. I fixed the test with a bounded retry (and proved it still catches real breakage by stubbing the promoter false) — but **that same bound means the overlay silently stops contributing to retrieval on a loaded machine in production too.** The comment shows it's a deliberate latency trade, so I left the product behavior alone rather than changing it uninvited.

Three property-based targets over the wire format, ~12M executions with no defect

and the reason is now written down where it will be read. Unknown newer-minor fields
pass through canonicalization ON PURPOSE — ADR 0001 makes 1.x additive-only, so an

field, so re-marshaling necessarily drops it; asserting round-trip equality over those
inputs would be asserting that tolerance is a bug.

which broke three tests including TestVerifyBytesToleratesUnknownFields. That test
answers the concern: the signature is taken over the bytes INCLUDING the unknown
fields, so an older reader can neither add nor strip what it does not understand and
still validate. The behavior was right; the missing piece was a comment saying why,

content.text:
Everything's on **#85** now. Local suite fully green; waiting on CI for the last two pushes.

## This round

**Fuzzed the wire format** — 12M+ executions across three property targets, since a byte-level codec used for signing is exactly where sampling-based unit tests miss things:
- canonical form is a **fixed point**, and every accepted output is re-acceptable and valid UTF-8
- the **struct path and bytes path agree**, so a signature made through one verifies through the other
- a signature verifies those bytes and **nothing else** — any flipped byte, stripped field, or appended data is rejected by error, never a panic

No defects found. That's a real result for code that had none of this coverage.

**I was wrong about a bug, and reverted myself.** My round-trip fuzzer flagged that `Canonicalize` passes unknown fields through while the struct path drops them. I read that as a canonicalization flaw plus a smuggling vector and changed it to reject — which broke three tests, one named `TestVerifyBytesToleratesUnknownFields`. That test answers the concern directly: the signature covers the unknown fields, so an older reader can neither add nor strip what it doesn't understand and still validate. The pass-through is **load-bearing** for ADR 0001's additive-only 1.x — a fatal unknown key would stop an older verifier validating a newer producer's artifact.

So I reverted, scoped my fuzzer to the property that actually holds, and wrote the reasoning into the code — the missing piece was never behavior, it was a comment explaining why.

**Fixed a documentation defect with teeth:** all 10 vendored `gitmeta` files named the *proof-of-concept* repo as their upstream. That PR was superseded, not merged; the shipping engine is in entire-api. As written it would send the next person to re-vendor from a dead branch. The header now records the real source, the two-way divergence since (api grew path-target support), and why it's currently inert — brain's engine only drives the bare local store at `refs/meta/local/main`, with no ref entire-api also writes.

**Verified inert, not assumed:** I checked for remotes/push/fetch in `factgitmeta` before calling the drift harmless.
